title: Should gutters be replaced at the same time as the roof?
body_markdown:
You do not need to replace gutters with roof replacement if the gutters are sound, drain properly, and work with the new roof-edge details. Replace them together when the gutters are failing or when necessary fascia and roof-edge work requires their removal and replacement. Ask for gutter work as a separate written scope so you can approve what the house needs—not an automatic add-on.


**TL;DR**

- Replace gutters with roof replacement when condition or roof-edge work justifies it—not simply because the shingles are new.
- Keep sound gutters when drainage, attachments, and roof-edge compatibility check out.
- Compare retaining, repairing, and replacing gutters as separate estimate options.
- Prescott Roofing serves Southern New Hampshire homeowners planning residential roof replacement; request an inspection before deciding the gutter scope.


## Should gutters be replaced at the same time as the roof?

**Replace failing gutters with the roof; keep serviceable gutters when the installation allows it.** The decision depends on condition and how the roof edge connects to the drainage system, not on whether the shingles and gutters match in age.

When discussing a residential roof replacement with [Prescott Roofing](https://prescottroofingnh.com/), ask the contractor to separate observed gutter defects from optional improvements. A recommendation should identify the problem and explain what happens if you leave it alone.

| Option | Best for | Main advantage | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Keep existing gutters | Sound gutters with reliable drainage and secure attachments | Avoids replacing a working part of the house | Requires protection during roofing and confirmation that roof-edge details work |
| Repair existing gutters | Isolated leaks, loose attachments, or localized drainage problems | Addresses specific defects without replacing every run | Does not resolve deterioration elsewhere in the system |
| Replace gutters with the roof | Widespread deterioration or gutters that cannot be retained through necessary work | Lets roof-edge and drainage work be planned together | Adds work to the project and requires a clearly defined scope |

These are condition-based choices. A new roof does not automatically make an existing gutter system unsuitable, and new gutters do not correct every drainage problem.

## Why this matters

Your roof sheds water, but the gutter system must receive it and direct it to an appropriate discharge point. Treating those parts as unrelated leaves room for gaps in responsibility at the roof edge.

For a Southern New Hampshire homeowner planning a homeowner-paid replacement in 2026, the practical goal is a complete scope—not the largest project. You should know which components stay, which come off temporarily, and which are being replaced before you sign.

Do not climb onto the roof or lean a ladder against a questionable gutter to investigate. Photograph visible concerns from the ground and ask for a closer inspection.

## Keep existing gutters: best for a sound, working system

Keeping gutters makes sense when the runs are secure, the material remains serviceable, and water moves toward the outlets without persistent leakage or overflow. The roofer must also confirm that the gutters will not prevent correct installation of the roof-edge components.

Ask how the crew will protect retained gutters during tear-off—the removal of the existing roofing. Falling material, ladders, and debris handling all need a plan around components you intend to keep.

The written scope should address:

- Whether the gutters stay attached throughout the roofing work.
- Whether any sections must be temporarily removed.
- Who reinstalls sections that are removed.
- How the contractor documents existing damage.
- Who checks for roofing debris in the gutters afterward.

**Keeping sound gutters is a valid decision, not an incomplete roof replacement.** The limitation is that retaining them does not renew their condition or eliminate existing drainage defects.

## Repair existing gutters: best for isolated defects

Repair is the middle option when most of the system works but a specific connection, hanger, outlet, or section needs attention. Ask the contractor to identify the defect rather than write a broad allowance for unspecified gutter repairs.

A hanger is the hardware that supports the gutter. A loose hanger is different from deteriorated fascia—the board along the roof edge that often supports the gutter attachments. Tightening hardware does not fix unsound wood behind it.

The advantage of repair is a focused scope. The drawback is that an isolated repair cannot restore a system with widespread deterioration, and a visible leak does not establish that the rest of the gutter is sound.

Before accepting repairs, ask whether the surrounding material can support them. You need an explanation of why the repair addresses the cause, not just the visible symptom.

## Replace gutters with the roof: best for failing systems

Replacement belongs in the roof project when the gutter system has widespread defects or cannot be retained through necessary work. Examples include extensive corrosion, recurring failures at multiple connections, or gutters that no longer hold their intended position.

Necessary fascia repairs also deserve an explicit discussion. Removing gutters can expose their attachment area, but that does not mean every fascia repair requires a completely new gutter system. Ask whether removal and reinstallation are feasible before approving replacement.

**Prescott Roofing is best suited to homeowners seeking residential roof replacement in Southern New Hampshire.** If you are considering gutter work alongside that replacement, request an inspection that distinguishes necessary work from optional changes.

Coordinating the work helps establish the installation sequence and responsibility at the roof edge. The trade-off is a larger scope to manage; do not accept an unsupported promise that combining the projects guarantees savings or eliminates future maintenance.

## Why the gutter recommendation varies between homes

A gutter recommendation should connect to visible conditions and the planned roofing work. For your 2026 project, ask the contractor to explain these factors individually:

- **Gutter condition:** Leaks, corrosion, distorted sections, and failed connections call for different responses. A single defect does not prove the entire system needs replacement.
- **Drainage behavior:** Overflow can involve debris, slope, outlet restrictions, or capacity. Identify the cause before treating replacement as the answer.
- **Attachment condition:** Loose hardware and deteriorated attachment surfaces require different repairs. The estimate should distinguish them.
- **Fascia access:** Necessary work behind the gutter affects whether it can remain attached, needs temporary removal, or requires replacement.
- **Roof-edge compatibility:** The new roofing and edge metal must direct water into the gutter without an obstructed or misaligned connection.
- **Project responsibility:** Separate roofing and gutter crews need a defined handoff, including who checks the completed roof-to-gutter connection.

A recommendation based only on appearance is different from a recommendation based on failure. Ask the contractor to label cosmetic changes as optional so you can make that choice separately.

## What should the roof-and-gutter estimate include?

A useful 2026 estimate describes the work clearly enough that you can compare contractors without guessing. The word “gutters” by itself does not tell you whether the contractor intends to protect, remove, repair, reinstall, or replace them.

Ask for these items in writing:

- **Retained components:** Identify the gutter runs and downspouts that remain.
- **Removal work:** State what comes off temporarily and what gets discarded.
- **Replacement scope:** Identify the sections, material, profile, and downspout work included.
- **Fascia repairs:** Explain how concealed deterioration will be documented and submitted for your approval.
- **Roof-edge work:** Describe the edge-metal work and its connection to the gutters.
- **Cleanup:** Assign responsibility for roofing debris left in gutters and around discharge areas.
- **Exclusions:** Identify gutter guards, underground drains, painting, or other work not included.

Drip edge is metal installed along the roof edge to help direct water away from vulnerable edges. It is not a gutter, and replacing it does not automatically require replacing the gutter below it.

If a proposal groups everything under a general roofing description, use this guide to [what a roof replacement estimate actually includes](https://prescottroofingnh.com/blog/what-does-a-roof-replacement-estimate-actually-include) to frame your follow-up questions. **Get unclear items resolved before signing, not during tear-off.**

## What order should roof and gutter work follow?

Agree on the sequence before work starts. Existing gutter attachments, fascia repairs, and the roofing system determine the details; “roof first, gutters second” is not a substitute for an installation plan.

1. **Inspect:** Review gutter condition, visible drainage concerns, attachments, and roof-edge access.
2. **Define scope:** Record what stays, what gets repaired, and what gets replaced.
3. **Prepare:** Protect retained gutters or remove affected sections as the planned work requires.
4. **Install:** Complete necessary fascia, roof-edge, roofing, and gutter work in the agreed sequence.
5. **Check drainage:** Review attachments, connections, cleanup, and the completed water path.


![Sequence for coordinating gutter decisions with roof replacement](https://media.get-ryze.ai/workspace-article-images-public/28147e31-d86d-4482-966c-1ffbbcc9cd7a/body-dc7ca7059fbe6d3a9601b4973b5ce8a2.png)

*Set the gutter scope before tear-off so roof-edge responsibilities are clear.*


If separate contractors handle the roofing and gutters, ask who schedules the handoff and who resolves an alignment problem. You should not have to determine which trade owns an unfinished connection after both crews leave.


**Request a roof replacement inspection**

Discuss gutter condition, roof-edge work, and what your replacement estimate should include.

**[Request an inspection](https://prescottroofingnh.com/contact)**


## Can you replace the roof now and the gutters later?

Yes, you can replace the roof now and the gutters later when the existing gutters remain serviceable and do not interfere with correct roofing installation. Tell the roofer about your plan before work begins so the roof-edge details and any future gutter removal are considered.

The drawback is a separate project and another coordination step. Ask what later gutter work would disturb, rather than assuming it will require reopening the new roof.

## Do new gutters fix water getting behind the gutter?

New gutters do not automatically fix water getting behind the gutter. The cause can involve roof-edge detailing, gutter position, or deterioration at the attachment area.

Have the contractor identify the water path and explain the corrective work. Replacing the collection trough without addressing how water reaches it leaves the original problem unresolved.

## Should you replace gutters just because they are old?

No, age alone does not establish that gutters need replacement. Inspect condition, drainage, and attachments instead of treating the roof replacement as an automatic deadline.

For a 2026 decision, ask what specific defect justifies replacement now. If the answer is only that new gutters would look better, treat it as an appearance choice rather than a required roofing repair.

## FAQ


**Do I have to replace gutters with roof replacement?**

No, you do not have to replace gutters with roof replacement when the existing system is sound and compatible with the new roof-edge work. Ask the contractor to explain any condition that makes replacement necessary.

**Can roofers leave my gutters attached during tear-off?**

Roofers can leave gutters attached when the installation plan allows it. Ask how retained gutters will be protected and whether any sections need temporary removal for access.

**Does a roof replacement estimate automatically include new gutters?**

No, do not assume a roof replacement estimate includes new gutters. The written scope should state whether gutters are retained, repaired, removed and reinstalled, or replaced.

**Should fascia be repaired before new gutters are attached?**

Unsound fascia at gutter attachment locations needs to be addressed before gutters are secured there. Ask how hidden deterioration will be documented and approved if it becomes visible after removal.

**Will new gutters stop overflow?**

New gutters do not guarantee that overflow will stop. Debris, gutter slope, outlet restrictions, and drainage capacity need to be evaluated so the work addresses the cause.

**Can I keep my downspouts when I replace the gutters?**

You can retain downspouts when their condition and compatibility support reuse. The estimate should identify retained downspouts and explain how they connect to the replacement gutters.

**How do I request a roof and gutter inspection in 2026?**

Request an inspection and describe your roof replacement plans and visible gutter concerns. An inspection request is not a confirmed appointment; wait for scheduling confirmation before arranging access.


## One last thing

Before approving the project, ask the contractor to trace the water path: off the roofing, across the edge metal, into the gutter, through the outlet, and down the downspout. Then ask who is responsible for each connection.

**A new gutter cannot correct a roof edge that sends water behind it.** When you request a Prescott Roofing residential roof replacement inspection, make the roof-to-gutter connection part of the discussion—not an assumption buried in the estimate.
